splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions for withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. The outcome affects billions in potential employer obligations across thousands of multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund (below)

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the period during which violations can be adjudicated.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding because there is no statutory authorization for such tolling, and courts lack authority to extend punishment beyond the judgment's terms.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under §2244(b)(1) on re-raising claims in successive collateral attacks, or whether they need only satisfy §2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule. This affects the gatekeeping framework for thousands of federal prisoners seeking post-conviction relief.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to §2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that §2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive §2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond §2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to §2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that §2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners filing §2255 motions, so they need only satisfy §2255(h)'s own requirements for successive motions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether candidates can demonstrate Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting and ballot-counting rules. The split affects the ability to challenge election administration practices before elections occur versus forcing disputes to arise only post-election.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election based on competitive injury from allegedly unlawful ballot-counting procedures.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate does not have Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election absent a more concrete and particularized injury.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous sentencing guidelines in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretation of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity to resolve ambiguity in the defendant's favor. This split was highlighted and deepened after Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretation.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing the Commission's interpretation to control even if it expands criminal liability.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary (Application Note 1) can expand the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to the career-offender guideline, which adds conspiracy and attempt to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether it impermissibly expands the unambiguous guideline text. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and that inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as 'controlled substance offenses' for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 cannot expand the definition beyond the text, particularly after Kisor narrowed deference to agency interpretations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) or whether possessing any one is disqualifying. The split leads to dramatically different sentences for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on the circuit.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1).

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule covers substances not listed in the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled, or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of whether the substance is controlled under federal law. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State-law offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include state-law offenses even if the particular substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, finding no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Substance must be federally scheduled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the underlying substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's amendments to mandatory minimums) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement permitting it exceeds its authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law can serve as a basis — alone or in combination with other factors — for compassionate release. Some circuits hold that courts may consider such changes, while others hold that allowing this would circumvent Congress's decision not to make the changes retroactive. The 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) deepened the split.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, as this would effectively make non-retroactive provisions retroactive through judicial action.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that sentencing courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, especially when combined with other factors, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in asset value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This has significant implications for debtors who convert in good faith but whose property has appreciated in value.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A) and the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a), post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, not the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under the Bankruptcy Code's structure and the purpose of § 348(f), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor who converts in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose sentences upon revocation of supervised release to punish defendants for their violations, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to sanctioning the breach of trust and facilitating reentry.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible purposes of sentences imposed upon revocation of supervised release. Some circuits permit courts to punish defendants for the underlying violation conduct, while others hold that revocation sentences should address only the breach of the court's trust. The Sixth Circuit has been identified as being at the extreme of this split.

positions.label: Punishment for violation conduct is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly consider and punish the defendant's violation conduct when imposing sentences upon revocation of supervised release.

positions.label: Revocation sentence should address breach of trust, not punish violations
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should primarily address the defendant's breach of the court's trust and the need to facilitate reentry, rather than punishing the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the duration of custody (such as First Step Act time credit calculations) must proceed via habeas corpus or may use civil rights statutes like Bivens.
splits.description: Circuits have maintained a longstanding split on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging BOP decisions that affect the fact or duration of confinement, or whether such claims may also be cognizable under civil rights causes of action. The split has evolved in the context of First Step Act earned time credit disputes.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration-of-confinement claims
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges the fact or duration of confinement, including BOP decisions on prerelease custody and earned time credits, habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy.

positions.label: Civil rights or other statutory remedies may also be available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may use civil rights causes of action to challenge certain BOP decisions even when they affect release timing, particularly where habeas relief would be inadequate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an appeal from an order denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the longer civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal proceeding (triggering the shorter criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal proceedings, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether orders denying motions to seal medical records qualify for immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine. The D.C. Circuit held such orders are immediately appealable given the high-order value of medical privacy, while other circuits have been more restrictive in applying the doctrine to sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders generally are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine, as privacy interests can be vindicated through other means or on appeal from final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: Circuits have applied differing standards for evaluating discrimination claims against business operators, affecting hospitality, retail, and other service industries. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach to relevant legal questions, indicating a circuit split on standards for fair treatment, discrimination liability, and damages.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a broader standard for establishing discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially encompassing a wider range of conduct.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a narrower standard requiring more specific showings to establish discrimination claims in hospitality or business establishments.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
